docs.title: Heimdall Listener
docs.text:
Heimdall Listener is a passive network monitor for system administrators. It shows which hosts on a network segment still use the legacy name-resolution protocols and auto-discovery mechanisms that attack tools such as Responder, Inveigh, mitm6 and ntlmrelayx abuse to capture or relay credentials, so you can turn those protocols off and prove that you did.

It comes as two programs that share the same engine:

Program For Capture backend heimdall-listener Workstations with a desktop: GUI, live table, compare runs libpcap / Npcap heimdall-cli Headless servers, cloud VMs, Windows Server Core, scheduled sensors Linux: pure Go (static binary, no libpcap needed). Windows: Npcap

Nothing is ever transmitted. Both programs only open the interface for reading. No probes, no canary lookups, no responses.

docs.title: What it detects
docs.text:
Traffic Why it matters Abused by LLMNR queries (udp/5355, IPv4 and IPv6) Windows falls back to LLMNR when DNS fails; anyone on the segment can answer and harvest NTLM credentials Responder, Inveigh, ntlmrelayx NetBIOS Name Service queries and registrations (udp/137) Same fallback as LLMNR; broadcast to the whole subnet Responder, Inveigh mDNS queries (udp/5353, IPv4 and IPv6) Windows 10+ also falls back to mDNS; answers are trusted from any host Responder, Inveigh WPAD lookups over LLMNR/NetBIOS/mDNS/DNS and HTTP wpad.dat fetches A poisoned proxy auto-config lets the attacker demand credentials from every browser and service on the host Responder (WPAD), ntlmrelayx DHCPv6 Solicit (udp/546→547) Windows asks for DHCPv6 even on IPv4-only networks and accepts the first answer, which becomes its DNS server mitm6

Results are aggregated per host, protocol and name with counts and first/last seen times, instead of one row per packet. NetBIOS names are shown with their suffix, e.g. fileserver<20>.

docs.title: Passive poisoner detection
docs.text:
Because the engine also decodes responses, it flags hosts that behave like an attacker, without sending a single packet:

Alert Trigger llmnr-nbns-responder A host answers LLMNR/NetBIOS for a WPAD name (high), for 3+ different names within 10 minutes (high), or for a name nobody was seen asking for (medium) mdns-responder A host answers mDNS for a WPAD name (medium) or for 5+ different names (low; Bonjour reflectors do this legitimately) dhcpv6-server Any host sends DHCPv6 Advertise/Reply and is not listed with --trusted-dhcpv6 (high: the mitm6 signature) wpad-http-server A host serves wpad.dat (info), escalated to high when the same host also answered name lookups

Visibility caveat: LLMNR, NetBIOS and DHCPv6 responses are unicast to the victim. On a switched network the sensor only sees responses to its own lookups unless it listens on a mirror/SPAN port or an unswitched segment. mDNS responses are multicast and always visible.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Download the binaries from the releases page:

File Notes heimdall-listener-windows-amd64.exe GUI. Requires Npcap (also installed by Wireshark). Run as Administrator. heimdall-listener-linux-amd64 GUI. Requires libpcap (apt install libpcap0.8 or equivalent). Grant it capture rights with setcap (below) and run it as your normal user; do not sudo a desktop app, it loses access to your display. heimdall-cli-linux-amd64, heimdall-cli-linux-arm64 Headless. Static binary, nothing to install. Run with sudo or grant it CAP_NET_RAW. heimdall-cli-windows-amd64.exe Headless. Requires Npcap. Run from an elevated prompt. SHA256SUMS Checksums for all of the above.

No prebuilt macOS binaries are provided. Both programs build and run on macOS with the go install commands below (libpcap ships with the OS); run them with sudo, or install Wireshark's ChmodBPF to capture as your user.

Or build from source with Go 1.25+ (libpcap-dev is needed only for the GUI):

go install github.com/ZerkerEOD/heimdall-listener/cmd/heimdall-cli@latest       # headless, pure Go on Linux
go install github.com/ZerkerEOD/heimdall-listener/cmd/heimdall-listener@latest  # GUI, needs libpcap-dev and cgo

Capturing needs elevated privileges on every platform. On Linux grant them to the binaries once instead of using sudo (required for the GUI, since a desktop app started with sudo cannot reach your Wayland/X session; convenient for the CLI). Repeat after replacing a binary:

sudo setcap cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin+eip /usr/local/bin/heimdall-listener
sudo setcap cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin+eip /usr/local/bin/heimdall-cli

Viewing a saved run in the GUI needs no privileges at all (heimdall-listener run.json).

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• GUI tour: every toolbar icon, control, tab and column explained.
  • CLI reference: all commands, flags, output formats and exit codes.
  • heimdall-cli <command> --help prints the same information on the command line, and heimdall-cli completion bash|zsh|fish|powershell generates shell completion.

docs.title: Using the GUI
docs.text:
1. Pick the interface in the top-left selector and press ▶. Let it run for a while: hosts only show up when they broadcast, so a quiet network needs time.
  2. The table updates live. Click a column header to sort, use Show to filter by protocol, WPAD or Alerts, and the search box to filter by IP, name or MAC. Click a row for details and the exact Group Policy / registry / firewall steps to turn that protocol off on that host.
  3. Press ■ to stop. ✕ clears the results (it asks first if they are unsaved).
  4. Save run writes a JSON run file. Export writes a CSV of the rows or a per-host remediation report (text). Tick Export visible rows only to export just what the current filter shows.
  5. Open run loads a saved file (or start the program with the file as an argument).

Alerts are hard to miss: the Alerts tab shows a count badge (red icon when something is HIGH), a red banner appears above the tabs with the newest high/medium alert and a Show alerts button, the affected host's rows get a red marker, and your desktop gets a notification the first time each alert is raised. The Alerts tab itself lists every detection with evidence and what to do about it.

docs.title: Comparing runs
docs.text: Save a run before you change anything, remediate, capture again, then open the Compare tab: pick the baseline file and compare it against the live session or a second file. Pairs of (host, protocol) that disappeared are resolved; new pairs and new hosts are highlighted; unchanged pairs show which names were added (+) or went away (-). The diff can be exported as CSV or JSON for a change ticket.

docs.title: Using the CLI (headless servers)
docs.text:
heimdall-cli interfaces                          list capturable interfaces
heimdall-cli capture -i eth0                     live table until Ctrl-C, then a remediation summary
heimdall-cli capture -i eth0 -d 1h -o baseline.json --csv baseline.csv --summary baseline.txt
heimdall-cli capture -i eth0 --jsonl --quiet     one JSON line per event (for logs / SIEM)
heimdall-cli diff baseline.json after.json       what appeared, what was resolved, what persists
heimdall-cli export after.json --format summary  render a saved run (csv | summary | summary-csv | json)
heimdall-cli version                             version and capture backend

Alerts show up in a red block at the top of the live view as soon as they are raised, and are repeated on stderr after the capture ends (even with --quiet). capture exits with status 3 when a HIGH alert was raised, 2 when capture privileges are missing, so scripts can react. Use --no-color (or NO_COLOR) for plain output.

Full flag tables, output formats and exit codes are in docs/CLI.md.

capture accepts -i more than once to listen on several interfaces at the same time. On Windows the interface can be given by its friendly name (-i "Ethernet 2"). When stdout is not a terminal the live table is replaced by a status line every minute (--status-every). Exit code 2 means the process lacks capture privileges; the message tells you how to fix it on that OS.

A typical remediation loop:

sudo heimdall-cli capture -i eth0 -d 30m -o before.json --summary before.txt
#  ... disable LLMNR / NetBIOS via GPO, fix the wpad DNS record ...
sudo heimdall-cli capture -i eth0 -d 30m -o after.json
heimdall-cli diff before.json after.json

Run files are plain JSON (schema_version 1) and can be opened in the GUI on your workstation.

docs.title: Running as a service
docs.text:
heimdall-cli service run keeps capturing and writes run-<UTC stamp>.json snapshots plus a latest.json into the output directory at a fixed interval (default every 5 minutes, keeping the last 48). Add --rollover 24h to start a fresh aggregation every day instead of accumulating forever.

Linux (systemd):

sudo heimdall-cli service install -i eth0 --snapshot-interval 15m
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl enable --now heimdall-listener
ls /var/lib/heimdall-listener/

The unit runs as a dynamic, unprivileged user with only CAP_NET_RAW and CAP_NET_ADMIN, writes under /var/lib/heimdall-listener (its StateDirectory), and is sandboxed with ProtectSystem=strict. If you pass a different --out-dir, keep it under that state directory or relax the unit.

Windows (elevated prompt, Npcap installed):

heimdall-cli.exe service install -i "Ethernet0" --snapshot-interval 15m
sc start heimdall-listener
dir %ProgramData%\HeimdallListener

The service starts automatically, depends on the Npcap driver, logs start/stop events to the Windows Event Log and to heimdall.log in the output directory, and restarts on failure. heimdall-cli service uninstall removes the registration; snapshots are kept.

docs.title: Self-test
docs.text:
scripts/gen-test-traffic.py is a small test harness (not part of the listener) that transmits the lookups the tool is meant to catch, so you can verify a sensor on your own segment in a minute:

heimdall-cli capture -i eth0 -d 30s -o test.json             # terminal 1: start listening first
python3 scripts/gen-test-traffic.py eth0 full                # terminal 2, while the capture runs
heimdall-cli export test.json                                # LLMNR, NetBIOS, mDNS and DHCPv6 rows from this host
python3 scripts/gen-test-traffic.py eth0 responder           # during a second capture: raises llmnr-nbns-responder

full must run while a capture is already listening. responder makes this machine look like a poisoner, so the alert names this machine's own IP, not the gateway it answered to.

No network at hand? docs/sample-run.json is a synthetic run with a WPAD responder, a rogue DHCPv6 server and a few ordinary hosts. It needs no privileges to view, and it is what the screenshots show:

heimdall-listener docs/sample-run.json          # GUI: Live, Alerts and Compare with real data
heimdall-cli export docs/sample-run.json        # CLI: the remediation report for the same run

docs.title: Cloud and virtual networks
docs.text:
Azure VNets and AWS VPCs do not forward broadcast or multicast traffic. A sensor on a cloud VM therefore only sees the VM's own LLMNR/NetBIOS/mDNS/DHCPv6 requests and its unicast DNS/WPAD lookups. That is still useful for proving that a server image is clean and that proxy auto-detection is off, but it will not show you what other VMs in the subnet are doing. On-premises, VLANs and hypervisor virtual switches behave like normal segments.

If mDNS is repeated across VLANs for IoT devices, the source IP you see is the gateway or firewall doing the repeating. There is no way to recover the original host from the repeated packet; capture on the original VLAN instead.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Capture is passive and limited to the broadcast domain of the interface (or what a SPAN port mirrors).
  • HTTP wpad.dat detection inspects the first segment of plain HTTP on tcp/80 only.
  • The pure-Go Linux backend does not follow IPv6 extension headers and only supports the default filter; pass --filter only with the libpcap-based binaries.
  • Alert thresholds are deliberately conservative and are labelled as suspected; verify before acting.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
make test                     # unit tests (race detector)
make cli-linux-amd64          # static CLI
make cli-windows-amd64        # CLI for Windows (pure Go)
make gui-linux                # GUI for Linux (needs libpcap-dev, libgl1-mesa-dev, xorg-dev)
make gui-windows              # GUI for Windows, cross-compiled (needs gcc-mingw-w64 and `make tools`)
make dist                     # everything plus SHA256SUMS in dist/

CI runs vet, tests and all builds on every push; tagged v* releases are built and published by GitHub Actions.

docs.title: Disclaimer
docs.text: This software is provided "as is" without any warranty of any kind. It identifies traffic patterns that usually indicate a weakness or an attack; it can miss traffic and it can flag legitimate devices. Verify findings before acting on them. Use at your own risk.

docs.title: Bug reports, feature requests and support
docs.text: Issues and pull requests are welcome; this is a side project worked on as time allows. If it helped you disable a legacy protocol before a pentest or red team found it, you can support the work on Patreon. Supporters at the Foothold tier and above get priority triage on issues they open here, applied automatically by the supporter label.

docs.title: heimdall-cli reference
docs.text:
heimdall-cli is the headless Heimdall Listener. Every command prints detailed help with --help; this page collects all of it in one place. Nothing the tool does transmits a packet.

heimdall-cli [--no-color] <command> [flags]
Command Purpose interfaces List interfaces you can capture on capture Capture until Ctrl-C or a duration, then write files and a report diff Compare two run files: new, resolved, unchanged export Render a saved run as CSV, a remediation summary, or JSON service run / install / uninstall Long-running sensor with periodic snapshots version Version, commit and capture backend completion bash\|zsh\|fish\|powershell Shell completion script

Global flag: --no-color disables ANSI colour (the NO_COLOR environment variable does the same).

docs.title: Privileges and exit codes
docs.text:
Capturing needs raw-socket rights: sudo or, better, sudo setcap cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin+eip heimdall-cli on Linux (repeat after replacing the binary); an elevated prompt with Npcap installed on Windows.

Exit status Meaning 0 Finished normally 1 Error (bad arguments, unreadable file, capture failure); the message is on stderr 2 Missing capture privileges; a hint for this OS is printed 3 capture finished but at least one HIGH alert was raised (suspected poisoner or rogue DHCPv6 server)

docs.title: interfaces
docs.text:
heimdall-cli interfaces [--all] [--json]

Lists usable interfaces (up, not loopback, with a routable address) as NAME, DESCRIPTION, ADDRESSES, UP. --all includes loopback and address-less interfaces; --json prints the list as JSON. On Windows the DESCRIPTION column is the friendly name you can pass to -i.

docs.title: capture
docs.text:
heimdall-cli capture -i IFACE [-i IFACE...] [-d DURATION] [-o run.json] [flags]
Flag Default Meaning -i, --interface required Interface to capture on; repeat for several. Name, or Windows friendly name -d, --duration 0 (until Ctrl-C) Stop after this long, e.g. 30s, 30m, 2h -o, --output Write the run file (JSON). This is what diff and the GUI read --csv Write aggregated entries as CSV --summary Write the per-host remediation report (text) --summary-csv Write the per-host summary as CSV -q, --quiet off No live table, status lines or report. Alerts and wrote ... notices still print --jsonl off Stream one JSON object per event to stdout (no live table); combine with -q for logs/SIEM --no-promisc off Do not enable promiscuous mode (broadcast/multicast are still received) --filter the default BPF expression libpcap filter expression; only with the libpcap backend (GUI, Windows CLI) --trusted-dhcpv6 Comma-separated IPv6 addresses of legitimate DHCPv6 servers; suppresses the dhcpv6-server alert for them --status-every 1m Interval of the status line when stdout is not a terminal

What you see while it runs:

  • On a terminal: a live view redrawn every second. Top line: interfaces, backend, elapsed time. If any alert exists, a red framed ALERTS box comes next. Then counters (packets, events, hosts, kernel drops, decode errors, per-protocol totals) and a table of the aggregated entries sorted WPAD first, then most recent. Press Ctrl-C to stop early; results are still written.
  • Not on a terminal (cron, systemd, a pipe): one status line per --status-every on stderr.
  • With --jsonl: one JSON object per decoded event on stdout, fields time, source_ip, dest_ip, source_mac, protocol, kind, name, query_type, answers, wpad, detail.

When the capture ends: the remediation report is printed to stdout (unless -q or --jsonl), alert lines are printed to stderr, requested files are written, and the exit status reflects HIGH alerts.

Stopping: -d elapsed, Ctrl-C, or SIGTERM (so timeout and service managers work).

docs.title: diff
docs.text:
heimdall-cli diff BASELINE.json CURRENT.json [-f table|json|csv] [-o FILE]

Compares two run files. A pair is one host doing one protocol as one kind (query or response).

  • NEW: pairs present now but not in the baseline. (new host) marks a host absent from the baseline.
  • RESOLVED: pairs in the baseline that are gone now. This is your proof that a remediation worked. (host gone) marks a host that vanished entirely.
  • UNCHANGED: pairs in both; names added since the baseline are prefixed +, names gone -.
  • ALERTS: new, cleared and persisting alerts.

The header line counts pairs, hosts and WPAD-related pairs on each side. -f json gives the full structure (for tooling), -f csv one row per pair.

docs.title: export
docs.text:
heimdall-cli export RUN.json [-f summary|csv|summary-csv|json] [-o FILE]
Format Content summary (default) The remediation report: capture window and counters, exposure by protocol, alerts with evidence and advice, then every host with its protocols, names, WPAD involvement and the exact steps to turn each protocol off csv One row per aggregated entry: source_ip, source_mac, protocol, kind, name, wpad, query_types, answers, count, first_seen, last_seen summary-csv One row per host: protocols, WPAD flag, alerts, names, counts, first/last seen json The run file itself, re-sorted and pretty-printed

docs.title: service
docs.text:
service run is the foreground process that systemd or the Windows Service Control Manager starts. It keeps capturing and writes run-<UTC stamp>.json plus latest.json into --out-dir every --snapshot-interval, pruning to --retain files, with a final snapshot on shutdown. Logs go to --log-file (default <out-dir>/heimdall.log), and to stderr as well when run from a terminal.

heimdall-cli service run -i IFACE [flags]
heimdall-cli service install -i IFACE [flags]      # root / elevated
heimdall-cli service uninstall [--name NAME]      # root / elevated
Flag (run and install) Default Meaning -i, --interface required Interface(s) to capture on --out-dir /var/lib/heimdall-listener (Linux), %ProgramData%\HeimdallListener (Windows) Snapshot directory --snapshot-interval 5m How often to write a snapshot --retain 48 Snapshots to keep; 0 keeps all --rollover 0 (cumulative) Reset the aggregation after this long, e.g. 24h --log-file <out-dir>/heimdall.log Log file --no-promisc, --filter, --trusted-dhcpv6 As for capture --name heimdall-listener Service / unit name

install only:

Flag Meaning --force Replace an existing unit or service --exe Path to the binary the service should run (default: the one you are running) --unit-dir Linux: systemd unit directory (default /etc/systemd/system)

On Linux install writes a hardened unit (dynamic unprivileged user, only CAP_NET_RAW and CAP_NET_ADMIN, ProtectSystem=strict, state directory /var/lib/heimdall-listener with mode 0750) and prints the systemctl commands to enable it. On Windows it creates an automatic-start service that depends on the Npcap driver, registers an Event Log source and sets restart-on-failure. uninstall removes the registration and keeps the snapshots.

docs.title: Files
docs.text: Run files are JSON with schema_version: 1, tool and host metadata, the capture window and counters, entries (one per host/protocol/kind/name with counts and timestamps) and alerts. They are written atomically (temp file plus rename), so latest.json is always complete even while it is being replaced.

docs.title: Heimdall Listener GUI tour
docs.text: The desktop application has one window with a toolbar, a controls row, an alert banner (hidden until needed), three tabs and a status bar. Nothing it does transmits a packet.

docs.title: Toolbar (top row, left to right)
docs.text:
Icon Action Notes ▶ / ■ Start / Stop capture on the selected interface The icon flips while capturing. The interface selector is locked during a capture ✕ Clear results Stops the capture if running. Asks first if there are unsaved results. Also returns from "viewing a file" to a fresh live session 💾 (save) Save run Writes a JSON run file (default name heimdall-run-<date>-<time>.json). This is the file heimdall-cli diff and the Compare tab use 📂 (folder) Open run Loads a saved run read-only ("Viewing " in the status bar). Start a new capture with ✕ first 📄 (file) Export CSV One row per aggregated entry ☰ (list) Export summary The per-host remediation report as text ↻ (refresh) Compare Jumps to the Compare tab ⓘ (info, far right) About Version, capture backend, and the passive-only statement

You can also open a run file by starting the program with it as an argument: heimdall-listener run.json (no privileges needed for viewing). The screenshots on this page are heimdall-listener docs/sample-run.json, a synthetic run you can open yourself; they are rendered by HEIMDALL_SNAPSHOT_DIR=out HEIMDALL_SNAPSHOT_RUN=docs/sample-run.json go test ./cmd/heimdall-listener/internal/ui -run TestRenderViews.

docs.title: Controls row
docs.text:
• Interface: pick the interface to listen on. The last choice is remembered. Only usable interfaces (up, not loopback, with a routable address) are listed.
  • Show: filter the table. All, one protocol (LLMNR, NetBIOS, mDNS, DNS, DHCPv6, HTTP), WPAD (anything WPAD-related), or Alerts (only hosts that have an alert).
  • Search box: live text filter on source IP, name, MAC, protocol and answered addresses.
  • Export visible rows only: when ticked, CSV and summary exports contain just what the table shows after filtering; otherwise everything captured. The Save run action always saves everything.

docs.title: Alert banner
docs.text: Appears between the controls and the tabs as soon as a HIGH or MEDIUM alert exists: ⚠ N alert(s), newest: [HIGH] 10.0.0.66 Answered a WPAD name lookup, with a Show alerts button. The first time each alert is raised you also get a desktop notification. LOW and INFO alerts only count in the tab badge.

docs.title: Live tab
docs.text:
The table has one row per host + protocol + kind + name, not one per packet.

Column Meaning Source IP The host that sent the packet. A red marker on this cell means the host has an alert. Bold means WPAD-related Protocol LLMNR, NetBIOS, mDNS, DNS, DHCPv6 or HTTP, with a colour stripe per protocol Kind Query (the host asked for something) or Response (the host answered or offered something) Name The name involved. NetBIOS names carry their suffix (fileserver<20>); DHCPv6 shows the client FQDN or the message type; HTTP shows host/wpad.dat. Bold means WPAD-related Count How many times this was seen First seen / Last seen Local time of the first and latest packet
  • Click a column header to sort; click again to reverse. The arrow shows the current sort. The default is newest first.
  • Click a row to open it in the detail pane below the table. The selection survives refreshes and re-sorting.
  • The detail pane shows the full record (MAC, query types, answered addresses, both local and UTC timestamps, the last packet's description, the NetBIOS suffix meaning), any alerts for that host, why the protocol matters, and the exact Group Policy / registry / firewall steps to turn it off.
  • Drag the divider between table and detail pane to resize.

The table refreshes four times a second while capturing; the status bar once a second.

docs.title: Alerts tab
docs.text:
The tab title shows the count, e.g. Alerts (3), with a red icon when any alert is HIGH. The page lists every passive detection: severity, host, title, evidence sentence, the names involved, how often and when it was seen, and what to do about it. Rules:

Rule Fires when llmnr-nbns-responder A host answers LLMNR/NetBIOS for a WPAD name (HIGH), for 3+ different names in 10 minutes (HIGH), or for a name nobody was seen asking (MEDIUM) mdns-responder A host answers mDNS for a WPAD name (MEDIUM) or for 5+ different names (LOW) dhcpv6-server A host sends DHCPv6 Advertise/Reply (HIGH), unless listed as trusted wpad-http-server A host serves wpad.dat (INFO), HIGH when it also answered name lookups

docs.title: Compare tab
docs.text:
1. Baseline… picks the saved run from before your change.
  2. Current is the live session by default (Use live session), or a second file (Current file…).
  3. Compare fills the table. Show filters it to New, Resolved or Unchanged.
Status Meaning resolved (green stripe) In the baseline, gone now: the remediation worked new (red stripe) Not in the baseline. (new host) if the host itself is new unchanged In both. Names added since the baseline are prefixed +, names gone -

The summary line counts pairs, hosts, WPAD pairs and alerts new/cleared. Export diff CSV / JSON save the comparison for a change ticket.

docs.title: Status bar
docs.text: ● Capturing on wlan0 (libpcap) | 00:12:31 | packets 12,345 | hosts 17 | LLMNR 120 · NetBIOS 44 | ⚠ 2 alert(s). It reads Stopped, Starting, ● Capturing on … or Viewing <file>. Kernel drops appear here if the host cannot keep up.

docs.title: Closing
docs.text: Closing the window with unsaved results asks for confirmation. Window size and the chosen interface are remembered between runs.
